new_statements.quote: El tono alto implica un acento de intensidad que marca el núcleo silábico; pero, en algunas ocasiones, el acento puede ir en la última sílaba y coincidir con el tono bajo. En palabras de cuatro sílabas puede haber un acento primario y uno secundario, o dos acentos primarios. En palabras de cinco sílabas (por lo general, nombres compuestos), siempre hay dos acentos primarios: uno en la segunda sílaba de la palabra y otro en la penúltima, excepto unos pocos nombres que lo llevan en la última. [...] En bisílabas, el patrón más común es alto-bajo y solamente los términos de parentesco llevan el patrón bajo-alto.
new_statements.translation: High tone implies an intensity stress that marks the syllable nucleus; but on some occasions the stress can fall on the last syllable and coincide with low tone. In four-syllable words there may be one primary and one secondary stress, or two primary stresses. In five-syllable words (generally compound nouns) there are always two primary stresses: one on the second syllable of the word and another on the penult, except for a few nouns that carry it on the last syllable. [...] In disyllables the most common pattern is high-low, and only kinship terms carry the pattern low-high.
new_statements.citation: González de Pérez, María Stella. 2000. "Bases para el estudio de la lengua pisamira." In M. S. González de Pérez & M. L. Rodríguez de Montes (eds.), Lenguas indígenas de Colombia: una visión descriptiva, 373-394. Santafé de Bogotá: Instituto Caro y Cuervo.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is an intensity prominence riding on the high pitch of a three-level (H/M/L) pitch pattern that the author finds non-contrastive and 'almost predictable' from syllable count: disyllables H-L (stress on the first syllable; kinship terms L-H, i.e. final), trisyllables M-H-L (stress on the second syllable; rarely H-H-L), four-syllable words M-H-M-L, H-H-H-L or M-H-H-L (one primary plus one secondary, or two primaries), five-syllable words (mostly compounds) two primary stresses on the second syllable and the penult. Suffixation shifts the disyllabic H-L pattern one syllable rightward (['júkɨ] 'tree' → [jū'kɨgɨ]). No single fixed position covers all word lengths; the closest generalisation is high/stress on the second syllable in words of three or more syllables and on the first in disyllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four-syllable words: one primary and one secondary stress, or two primaries; five-syllable words: always two primary stresses (2nd syllable and penult). No further detail on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Kinship terms are L-H (final prominence) in 28 of 32 terms collected, but take the ordinary M-H-L pattern once affixed ([mã'kó] 'daughter' → [mã'kóŋã] 'little daughter' → [jɨ'mãkò] 'my daughter'); occasionally stress falls on the final syllable coinciding with low tone; a few five-syllable nouns carry the second primary stress on the last syllable; the trisyllabic H-H-L pattern is very rare; in CVV words and in vowel sequences with /a/ (or /o/) tone and stress 'vary in position arbitrarily' between mono- and bitonal renderings (p. 384). The author states the tone/stress analysis is unfinished (p. 382).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms elicited 1985-1989 at Yacayacá (Vaupés) and with an informant in Chía; pitch levels are non-contrastive within Pisamira (the author explicitly concludes it is not a tonal language, unlike other Tukanoan languages, and excludes tone from phonemic transcription), though lexical items differ from Bará/Tatuyo/Tucano cognates only in tone patterns (Cuadro 3). 'Very high' and 'very low' variants depend on position in the intonation contour.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Pisamira of Yacayacá (middle Vaupés, Colombia), the sole known community; the author identifies the group with Koch-Grünberg's 'Wasöna/Pisátapuyo' and Waltz & Wheeler's 'Pápiwa'. Ethnologue subsumes Pisamira under Tucano [tuo] (tuca1252), which Glottolog and Chacon 2014 reject; the statement applies to pisa1245 itself, not to Tucano.

new_statements.quote: Dado el foco principal de este trabajo, la descripción del acento y el tono será muy breve, haciendo solo un repaso general de lo que sabemos sobre este asunto [...] Por último, encontramos en el análisis de Valderrama (2014) sobre los tonos en pisamira en que los patrones tonales en la lengua dependen del número de sílabas y que el acento siempre se presenta en la sílaba de tono alto, se sugieren ciertas restricciones en la realización de los tonos pero no deja clara la función fonológica. [fn 24:] Gómez-Imbert (2011a, p. 1451) asegura que las lenguas tuyuca, desano, siriano, yurutí y pisamira presentan una sola mora A (tono alto) por palabra
new_statements.translation: Given the main focus of this work, the description of stress and tone will be very brief, only a general review of what we know about the matter [...] Finally, we find in Valderrama's (2014) analysis of the tones of Pisamira that the tonal patterns of the language depend on the number of syllables and that stress always falls on the high-tone syllable; certain restrictions on the realisation of tones are suggested but the phonological function is not made clear. [fn 24:] Gómez-Imbert (2011a, p. 1451) states that Tuyuca, Desano, Siriano, Yurutí and Pisamira have a single H (high-tone) mora per word

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's González-based record (stress coincides with the high-tone syllable) and adds, second-hand, that there is one H mora per word (culminativity) and, first-hand, that compound verbs have a single primary accent; it supplies no placement of its own and does not supersede González 2000 §3.1.3.2. Its handle URL https://repositorio.unb.br/handle/10482/32532 could not be reached by automated download on two attempts
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis gives no placement rule of its own: §2.5 is a literature review that juxtaposes González 2000 (pitch is a syllable feature with no phonological value; Pisamira not tonal), Ardila 2004 (a 'particular accentuation' marking a transition away from the Eastern Tucanoan tonal system), Valderrama 2014 (tone patterns depend on syllable count; stress always on the high-tone syllable) and Gómez-Imbert 2011a (one H mora per word, i.e. culminative), and then defers the topic to future research. The author's own remarks: p. 76 fn 44 'mis análisis preliminares de la fonología no abarcan discusiones sobre acento, tono y entonación'; p. 95 compound verbs V1+V2 are one phonological word and 'poseen un solo acento primario'; p. 154 tonal distinctions were corroborated empirically but are not described.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing of its own; the only remark is that V1+V2 compound verbs carry a single primary accent (p. 95).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated by the author; the sources she reviews disagree on whether tone is phonological (González: no; Valderrama/Gómez-Imbert: tone patterns with one H per word).
new_statements.identity_note: Both works are the same 2018 UnB MA thesis by Iveth Patricia Rodríguez Preciado (surname order as on the UnB file and oasisbr; the target list has it inverted), on Pisamira as spoken at Yacayacá on the Vaupés river, Colombia; the catalog's source González de Pérez 2000 describes the same community. No other dialect is distinguished.

new_statements.quote: En la composición verbal VERBO[1] + VERBO[2] en pisamira ambas raíces se encuentran fonológicamente integradas pues los hablantes las reconocen como una sola palabra; además, poseen un solo acento primario y obedecen a las reglas y restricciones morfofonológicas de la lengua. [p. 94-95] ... Dejamos para investigaciones futuras la descripción de las distinciones tonales dado que, aunque empíricamente pude corroborar su existencia, requieren de un amplio abordaje tipológico que proponga análisis sistemáticos que por ahora exceden el alcance de los objetivos de la presente pesquisa. [p. 154]
new_statements.translation: In VERB[1] + VERB[2] verbal compounding in Pisamira both roots are phonologically integrated, since speakers recognise them as a single word; moreover, they have a single primary accent and obey the morphophonological rules and restrictions of the language. [pp. 94-95] ... We leave for future research the description of the tonal distinctions, since, although I was able to corroborate their existence empirically, they require a broad typological approach with systematic analyses that for now exceed the scope of the present study. [p. 154]

readall_conflicts: The thesis itself contains no placement claim, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's disyllable/trisyllable pattern (penultimate stress, from González de Pérez 2000 §3.1.3.2). The disagreement it documents is between its sources on the TYPE of system: González 2000 (the catalog's source) finds pitch to be a syllable feature with no phonological value and says Pisamira is probably not tonal, whereas Valderrama 2014 (Univalle, not obtained) describes tone patterns that depend on syllable count with stress always on the high-tone syllable, and Gómez-Imbert 2011a (p. 1451) groups Pisamira with Tuyuca, Desano, Siriano and Yurutí as one-H-mora-per-word languages; Ardila 2004 (cited but absent from the bibliography) calls it a transition away from the Eastern Tucanoan tonal system. All agree that the stressed syllable is the high-pitched one. A minor tension: González says five-syllable compound nouns always have two primary accents, while the thesis (p. 95) says V1+V2 compound verbs have a single primary accent; different word classes, so not a direct contradiction.
